🐾 Here’s the story behind Matt’s payments work at **JP Morgan Chase**.

From **August 2009 to June 2012**, Matt served as Technology Delivery Lead for ACCESS Next Generation, the bank’s global corporate banking portal. Its treasury operations relied on separate regional systems, while Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform needed custom engineering to meet the bank’s payment, security, and compliance requirements. Corporate treasurers faced separate local logins and regional payment systems. Client administrators spent days manually configuring permissions.

Matt managed a blended team of **40+** **Accenture** and bank resources across Mumbai, Bangalore, and the US. He spent **70 to 80%** of his time embedded at Bottomline’s Portsmouth offices, managing where the platform’s native capabilities ended and bank-specific development was required.

He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and government tax payment modules, including NACHA file validation, foreign exchange integration, and Message Authentication Code security so users could verify payment integrity before release. Contextual help explained wire formatting, tax payment codes, and FX parameters directly within payment workflows.

He also delivered the centralized payments gateway, handling message transformation, protocol translation, and routing across **12 countries**. For administrators, he replaced individual permission configuration with role-based profiles, bulk changes across users and accounts, and a centralized dashboard. Entitlement management dropped from days to minutes.

Alongside that engineering, Matt led payments data migration without disruption to live payment operations. He coordinated jurisdiction-specific data visibility and access controls across APAC, EMEA, and the Americas, and owned production incident response, root-cause analysis, and live status communications.

ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, consolidating regional systems into a unified portal serving **135,000+** corporations, financial institutions, governments, and municipalities across **180+ countries**. Corporate treasurers gained a single entry point for payments across regions, real-time global reporting, and single sign-on across treasury functions.

🐾 Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose.

Many engineering teams he inherited were “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” Teams avoided risks because they feared blame, while hierarchical structures and silos between engineering, design, and product slowed delivery. His focus was to create an environment where people could speak honestly, challenge assumptions, and make decisions close to the work.

Matt makes intent explicit, uses transparency and direct feedback, and coaches teams to think clearly rather than just execute tasks. At the **Accenture** Cloud Innovation Center, he assembled balanced teams of engineers, product managers, and UX architects with equal participation and shared accountability. He connected team goals to client and business outcomes, introduced pair programming and collaborative coding, and used stand-ups, retrospectives, and knowledge-sharing sessions to identify roadblocks. Teams could voice feedback and implement changes autonomously.

His “permit to fail” philosophy meant non-punitive post-mortems and lean, low-stakes experiments, not pointing fingers. In innovation engagements, he set expectations upfront that prototypes and user tests would likely fail. Teams used those results to challenge assumptions and shape product direction week by week, before committing to costly builds. He also chooses work environments around psychological safety, clear purpose, integrity, and respect, with a focus on outcomes rather than optics.

At the Cloud Innovation Center, teams accelerated delivery **4x** after embracing lean product and modern engineering practices. The balanced-team work also reduced handoffs and project delays and achieved **zero-defect production code** through iterative development and real-time feedback loops.

Matt built the Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers to address both problems, with full P&L accountability, hiring, training, and delivery responsibility.

He brought product managers, designers, and engineers together in balanced teams. Instead of separate development and QA phases, teams used pair programming, test-driven development, and automated pipelines. They delivered thin-slice, production-ready solutions and gathered user feedback. The talent program recorded near-zero attrition in its first **2 years**.

He rebuilt stories with defined scenarios and brought experts alongside engineers for hands-on coaching. The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see.

The CIC grew from **0 to 150+ practitioners**, delivering **30+ product engagements** across **15+ Fortune 500 clients**, with **4X faster velocity** and zero-defect deployments. Delivery excellence and customer relationships drove **\$100M+ in repeat business**. At **JP Morgan**, Matt’s payments and Salesforce platforms each rolled out across **12 countries**. answer_md:
🐾 Here’s a time Matt’s assumptions led to a production-data incident.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a **Fortune 500** financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. He relied on that documentation rather than confirming its accuracy. He did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, verify whether production customer data had been masked, or implement compensating controls such as email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They identified insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed from downstream environments. He worked collectively with the team to understand what happened and implement corrective controls.

The client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described it as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence,” and acknowledged that these were assumptions he should have verified rather than inherited.

His stated lesson was that “assumptions are risks in disguise.” IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach.

IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. He relied on that documentation rather than confirming its accuracy. He did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, verify whether production customer data had been masked, or implement compensating controls such as email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They identified insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed from downstream environments. 🐾 Here’s how Matt built AWS Launchpad.

At **Accenture’s** Liquid Studio, traditional training programs couldn’t keep pace with rapidly evolving AWS technologies. Engineers had gaps in cloud competency, and cloud adoption was slowing. The Atlanta Innovation Hub needed a structured cloud enablement program that prepared engineers for cloud-native application development, not just certification exams.

From **July 2018 to November 2019**, Matt led AWS Launchpad in collaboration with AWS. He designed structured learning paths and certification programs around AWS core services, including Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB, Kubernetes, and ECS/Fargate. The program connected certification preparation with practical work in cloud-native application development.

Instead of relying on theory alone, Matt delivered interactive workshops and hands-on labs that immersed engineers in real-world AWS environments. Engineers could apply the services they were studying rather than only learning their definitions and exam requirements.

He also established cloud expert mentorship teams to embed AWS best practices and retain institutional knowledge. Group coaching sessions and knowledge-sharing workshops gave participants opportunities to learn together, with support beyond the individual coursework. The combination was structured learning paths, practical application, and mentor-based training.

More than **200 professionals** earned AWS certifications, including Solutions Architect and DevOps Engineer certifications. The program accelerated cloud adoption and the launch of cloud-native initiatives across **Accenture**, while establishing ongoing mentorship and knowledge-sharing practices for continued learning.
